L144: # Student Visa
L145: ## Overview
L146: 
L147: Generally, foreign nationals who wish to travel to the United States must first obtain a visa, either a nonimmigrant visa for a temporary stay, or an immigrant visa for permanent residence. You must have a student visa to travel to the United States to study. Your course of study and the type of school you plan to attend determine whether you need an F visa or an M visa.
L148: To enter the United States to attend:  | You need the following visa category:
L149: --- | ---
L150: University or college  | F
L151: High School
L152: ---
L153: Private elementary school
L154: ---
L155: Seminary
L156: ---
L157: Conservatory
L158: ---
L159: Another academic institution, including a language training program
L160: ---
L161: Vocational or other recognized nonacademic institution, other than a language training program  | M
L162: Students cannot travel on the Visa Waiver Program or with Visitor Visas
L163: You must have a student visa (F or M visa) to travel to the United States to study. You may not study after entering on a visitor (B) visa, unless you are eligible for and have obtained a change of status from USCIS, or through the Visa Waiver Program (VWP), except to undertake recreational (non-credit) study as part of a tourist visit. For more information on the VWP, see 【34†Visa Waiver Program】.
L164: For short periods of recreational study, a Visitor (B) visa may be appropriate
L165: A visitor (B) visa permits enrollment in a short recreational course of study, which is not for credit toward a degree or academic certificate. Learn more about 【35†Visitor Visas】.
L166: Study leading to a U.S. conferred degree or certificate is not permitted on a visitor (B) visa, even if it is for a short duration. For example, a student in a distance learning program that  requires a period of time on the institution’s U.S. campus must obtain a student (F or M) visa prior to entering the United States.
L167: Student Acceptance at a SEVP Approved School
L168: The first step to studying in the United States is apply to a SEVP-approved school in the United States.  If the SEVP-approved school accepts your enrollment, you will be registered for the 【36†Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS)†www.ice.gov】 and must pay the SEVIS I-901 fee.  The SEVP-approved school will issue you a Form I-20.  After you receive the Form I-20 and register in SEVIS, you may apply at a U.S.
L169: Embassy or Consulate for a student (F or M) visa.  You must present the Form I-20 to the consular officer when you attend your visa interview.
L170: If your spouse and/or children will live with you in the United States while you study, they must also enroll in SEVIS, obtain individual Form I-20s from the SEVP-approved school, and apply for a visa (but they do not pay the SEVIS fee).
L171: 
L172: Visit the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) 【37†Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP)†www.ice.gov】 website to learn more about SEVIS and the SEVIS I-901 Fee.
L173: Visit the Department of State 【38†EducationUSA†educationusa.state.gov】 website to learn about educational opportunities for undergraduate and graduate study, and an overview of the application process.  You can also visit the DHS 【39†Study in the States†studyinthestates.dhs.gov】 school search page to search for SEVP-certified schools.
L174: ## How To Apply
L175: 
L176: There are several steps to apply for a visa. The order of these steps and how you complete them may vary by U.S. Embassy or Consulate. Please consult the instructions on the 【10†embassy or consulate website†www.usembassy.gov】.
L177: ## Complete the Online Visa Application
L178: 
L179:   * Online Nonimmigrant Visa Application, 【40†Form DS-160†ceac.state.gov】 – 【41†Learn more】 about completing the 【40†DS-160†ceac.state.gov】. You must: 1) complete the online visa application, and 2) print the application form confirmation page to bring to your interview.
L180:   * Photo –You will upload your photo while completing the online Form DS-160. Your photo must meet the 【42†Photograph Requirements】.
L181: ## Schedule an Interview
L182: 
L183: Interviews are generally required for visa applicants with certain limited exceptions. Consular officers may require an interview of any visa applicant.
L184: You should schedule an appointment for your visa interview at the 【10†U.S. Embassy or Consulate†www.usembassy.gov】 in the country where you live. You may schedule your interview at another U.S. Embassy or Consulate, but be aware that it may be more difficult to demostrate that you qualify for a visa outside of the country where you live.
L185: Wait times for interview appointments vary by location, season, and visa category, so you should apply for your visa early. Review the interview wait time for the location where you will apply:
L186: 
L187: * * *
L188: 
L189: New Students – Student (F and M) visas for new students can be issued up to 365 days before the start date of a course of study.  However, you will not be allowed to enter the United States on your student visa more than 30 days before the start date.
L190: Continuing Students - Student (F and M) visas for continuing students may be issued at any time, as long as the student is currently enrolled at a SEVP-approved school or institution and in SEVIS.  Continuing students may enter the United States at any time before classes start.
L191: ## Prepare for Your Interview
L192: 
L193:   * Fees - Pay the non-refundable visa application fee, if you are required to pay it before your interview. If your visa is approved, you may also pay a visa issuance fee, if applicable to your nationality. Fee information is provided below:
L194: 
L195: ## Application Fee
L196: 
L197: $185
L198: ### Select your nationality to see Issuance Fee
L199: 
L200: [Input: Select a country/authority or area]
L201: 
L202: 【43†All Fees】
L203: 
L204: * * *
L205: 
L206:   * Review the instructions available on the website of the 【10†U.S. Embassy or Consulate†www.usembassy.gov】 where you will apply to learn more about fee payment.
L207: ## Gather Required Documentation
L208: 
L209: Gather and prepare the following required documents before your visa interview:
L210:   * Passport valid for travel to the United States – Your passport must be valid for at least six months beyond your period of stay in the United States (unless exempt by 【44†country-specific agreements†www.cbp.gov】). Each individual who needs a visa must submit a separate application, including any family members listed in your passport.
L211:   * Nonimmigrant Visa Application, 【45†Form DS-160】 confirmation page.
L212:   * Application fee payment receipt, if you are required to pay before your interview.
L213:   * Photo – You will upload your photo while completing the online Form DS-160. If the 【46†photo upload fails,】 you must bring one printed photo in the format explained in the 【42†Photograph Requirements】.
L214:   * Certificate of Eligibility for Nonimmigrant (F-1) Student Status-For Academic and Language Students, Form I-20 or Certificate of Eligibility for Nonimmigrant (M-1) Student Status for Vocational Students, Form I-20 – Your school will send you a Form I-20 once they have entered your information in the SEVIS database. You and your school official must sign the Form I-20.  All students must be registered in the Student and Exchange Visitor System (SEVIS).
L215: Your spouse and/or minor children, if they intend live in the United States with you, will each receive an individual Form I-20.
L216: ### Additional Documentation May Be Required
L217: 
L218: A consular officer will interview you to determine your qualifications for a student visa, and may request additional documents, such as evidence of:
L219:   * Your academic preparation, such as:
L220:     * Transcripts, diplomas, degrees, or certificates from schools you attended; and
L221:     * Standardized test scores required by your U.S. school;
L222:   * Your intent to depart the United States upon completion of the course of study; and
L223:   * How you will pay all educational, living and travel costs.
L224: 
L225: Review the instructions for how to apply for a visa on the website of the 【10†U.S. Embassy or Consulate†www.usembassy.gov】 where you will apply.
L226: ## Attend Your Visa Interview
L227: 
L228: A consular officer will interview you to determine whether you are qualified to receive a student visa. You must establish that you meet the requirements under U.S. law to receive a visa.
L229: 
L230: Ink-free, digital fingerprint scans are taken as part of the application process. They are usually taken during your interview, but this varies based on location.
L231: After your visa interview, the consular officer may determine that your application requires further 【47†administrative processing】.  The consular officer will inform you if this is required.
L232: 
L233: After the visa is approved, you may need to pay a visa issuance fee (if applicable to your nationality), and make arrangements for the return of the passport and visa to you.  Review the 【48†visa processing times】 to learn more.
L234: ## Entering the United States
L235: 
L236: A visa does not guarantee entry into the United States.  A visa only allows a foreign citizen to travel to a U.S. port-of-entry (generally an airport) and request permission to enter the United States. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officials at the port-of-entry have authority to permit or deny admission to the United States.
L237: After you present your passport, visa, and Form I-20 at the port-of-entry, a CBP official will make this decision.  Upon admission, the CBP official will provide an admission stamp or paper Form I-94, Arrival/Departure Record.
L238: Learn about procedures for students (with F or M visas) entering the United States on the CBP website under 【49†Arrival Procedures for Students or Exchange Visitors†www.cbp.gov】.  Learn about admissions and entry requirements, restrictions about bringing food, agricultural products, and other restricted/prohibited goods, and more by reviewing the 【49†CBP website†www.cbp.gov】.
L239: ## Extending Your Stay
L240: 
L241: Foreign students in the United States with F visas must depart the United States within 60 days after the program end date listed on Form I-20, including any authorized practical training.
L242: Foreign students may request an extension through U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) website (see the USCIS 【50†Extend Your Stay†www.uscis.gov】 page). Additional information to maintain student status is on the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement SEVP website under 【51†Maintaining Your Immigration Status While a Student or Exchange Visitor†studyinthestates.dhs.gov】.
L243: Failure to depart the United States on time will result in being 【52†out of status】. Under U.S. law, visas of individuals who are out of status are automatically voided (【53†Section 222(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act†www.uscis.gov】).  Any multiple entry visa that was voided due to being out of status will not be valid for future entries into the United States.
L244: Failure to depart the United States on time may also result in you being ineligible for visas in the future in certain cases. Review 【54†Visa Denials】 and 【55†Ineligibilities and Waivers: Laws】 to learn more.
L245: ## Change of Status
L246: 
L247: If your plans change while in the United States (for example, you marry a U.S. citizen or receive an offer of employment), you may be able to request a change in your nonimmigrant status to another category through U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). See 【56†Change My Nonimmigrant Status†www.uscis.gov】 on the USCIS website to learn more.
L248: While you are in the United States, receiving a change of status from USCIS does not require you to apply for a new visa.  However, once you depart the United States you must apply for a new visa at a U.S. Embassy or Consulate in the appropriate category for your travel.
L249: ## Additional Information
L250:   * There is no guarantee you will be issued a visa. Do not make final travel plans or buy tickets until you have a visa.
L251:   * For information about working in the United States during your study, review 【57†Students and Employment†www.uscis.gov】 and Form I-765 【58†Work Authorization Instructions†www.uscis.gov】 on the USCIS website.
L252:   * If you have a temporary break in your study, view the information on the SEVP website under 【59†Do Students Returning from Temporary Absences Need New Visas?†studyinthestates.dhs.gov】 If your student visa is still valid, but you are outside the United States, you should consult with your Designated School Officials.

L1076@P42: ¶ 17. Declining international student enrollment will have substantial financial, educational,

L1078@P42: 788 F. Supp. 3d 70, 95 (D. Mass. 2025) (finding irreparable harm, as organization’s “core

L1080@P42-43: Case 1:26-cv-13799-FDS Document 50 Filed 09/14/26 Page 43 of 4844
L1081@P43: Second, international students who do enroll in U.S. colleges and universities will face
L1082@P43: complications, such as those associated with enrolling for joint or combined degrees. Institutions
L1083@P43: are already being forced to choose between changing such programs or being unable to offer
L1084@P43: them to international students. See, e.g., Ex. 19, Dkt. No. 2-19, at ¶ 33. Moreover, due to the
L1085@P43: Final Rule, many international students already lawfully present in the United States are
L1086@P43: concerned about traveling internationally, leading to students canceling international research or
L1087@P43: travel to conferences. See, e.g., Ex. 11, Dkt. No. 2-11, at ¶ 27. Universities whose students
L1088@P43: cannot travel will be unable to operate those programs or may have to restructure them.
L1089@P43: Finally, by DHS’s account, universities will endure substantial administrative burdens to
L1090@P43: comply with the final rule. DHS has estimated that “DSOs and ROs will have to spend
L1091@P43: approximately 135 hours for rule familiarization and adaptation in the first year after the rule
L1092@P43: takes effect,” with costs up to $267.9 million. 91 Fed. Reg. at 45058. At a minimum, the
L1093@P43: upheaval from the Final Rule constitutes irreparable harm. See, e.g., Doe v. Trump, 157 F.4th
L1094@P43: 36, 79 (1st Cir. 2025) (noting that “administrative upheaval” constitutes irreparable harm).
L1095@P43: In short, plaintiffs have clearly demonstrated that immediate irreparable harm will occur
L1096@P43: if a preliminary injunction is not issued.
L1097@P43: C. Balance of Equities
L1098@P43: Finally, the public interest weighs heavily in favor of providing relief. There are
L1099@P43: currently approximately 1.6 million students and dependents in F status, 504,000 J
L1100@P43: nonimmigrants, and 24,000 I nonimmigrants. 91 Fed. Reg. at 45116.
L1101@P43: As the Clemens study notes, in 2023-2024, international students contributed $44 billion
L1102@P43: to the economy and directly supported nearly 400,000 jobs, one job for every three international
L1103@P43: students. Ex. 21, Dkt. No. 2-24, at 2. Moreover, as other commenters explained, of the
L1104@P43: immigrants who founded high-potential startups backed by venture capital, 75% came to the
L1105@P43-44: Case 1:26-cv-13799-FDS Document 50 Filed 09/14/26 Page 44 of 4845
L1106@P44: United States as international students, and approximately 44% of immigrant Nobel Laureates in
L1107@P44: academic disciplines attended United States institutions for their highest educational degree. Ex.
L1108@P44: 2, Dkt. No. 2-24, at 6; Ex. 3, Dkt. No. 2-24, at 5.
L1109@P44: Nonimmigrants with F and J visas also make important contributions to their
L1110@P44: communities through clinical and field work. For example, as commenters noted,
L1111@P44: “approximately 16,000 medical residents and fellows were in J-1 status in 2024, comprising
L1112@P44: roughly 10% of resident physicians in the US.” Ex. 6, Dkt. No. 2-24, at 8. Those J-1 physicians
L1113@P44: “often serve in rural and medically underserved areas of the US,” and often “go on to pursue
L1114@P44: additional training in medical specialties that are much needed in the US,” meaning they “serve a
L1115@P44: critical role in the US healthcare infrastructure.” Id.
L1116@P44: Finally, international journalists make significant contributions to the United States, in
L1117@P44: particular, contributing to the open exchange of information, ideas, and opinions that are the
L1118@P44: hallmarks of a free and democratic society. See, e.g., Grosjean v. Am. Press Co., 297 U.S. 233,
L1119@P44: 250 (1936). (“A free press stands as one of the great interpreters between the government and
L1120@P44: the people. To allow it to be fettered is to fetter ourselves.”).
L1121@P44: The Final Rule directly threatens those benefits to the substantial detriment of the
L1122@P44: American public. Moreover, postponing the effective date of the Final Rule would not harm the
L1123@P44: public interest because, as explained above, it is not reasonably related to any legitimate DHS
L1124@P44: objective. The balance of equities and the public interest thus strongly favor the issuance of a
L1125@P44: preliminary injunction.
L1126@P44: D. Conclusion
L1127@P44: Accordingly, plaintiffs have demonstrated a substantial likelihood of success on the
L1128@P44: merits of their claims; that immediate irreparable harm will ensue if the Final Rule is not
L1129@P44: enjoined; and that the balance of the equities and the public interest favor issuance of a
L1130@P44-45: Case 1:26-cv-13799-FDS Document 50 Filed 09/14/26 Page 45 of 4846
L1131@P45: preliminary injunction. The Court will therefore issue such an injunction staying the operation
L1132@P45: of the rule.
L1133@P45: E. Scope of Relief
L1134@P45: The remaining issue is the proper scope of relief. Plaintiffs seek vacatur under 5 U.S.C.
L1135@P45: § 706 or in the alternative, postponement under 5 U.S.C. § 705. Under the circumstances, while
L1136@P45: vacatur under § 706 may ultimately prove to be appropriate, the Court will take the more
L1137@P45: cautious approach of postponing the effective date of the Final Rule. The question then becomes
L1138@P45: whether, under § 705, the Court should issue a narrower order specifically tailored to plaintiffs or
L1139@P45: a broader order staying the Final Rule.
L1140@P45: Section 705 of the APA states that “[o]n such conditions as may be required and to the
L1141@P45: extent necessary to prevent irreparable injury, the reviewing court . . . may issue all necessary
L1142@P45: and appropriate process to postpone the effective date of an agency action.” Defendants contend
L1143@P45: that § 705, as evidenced by its use of “necessary and appropriate,” directs courts to apply
L1144@P45: traditional equitable principles. Therefore, defendants assert, under the Supreme Court’s
L1145@P45: decision in Trump v. Casa, Inc., that relief must be limited to parties before the court. 606 U.S.
L1146@P45: 831, 837 (2025) (holding that universal injunctions “likely exceed the equitable authority that
L1147@P45: Congress has granted to federal courts” in the Judiciary Act of 1789).
L1148@P45: The prevailing view, however, is that the authority to grant relief under the APA is not
L1149@P45: coextensive with the equitable authority granted under the Judiciary Act of 1789. See
L1150@P45: Massachusetts v. Dep’t of Educ., 831 F. Supp. 3d 34, 49-51 (D. Mass. 2026). Section 706 of the
L1151@P45: APA authorizes a reviewing court to “set aside agency action” found to be unlawful. 5 U.S.C.
L1152@P45: § 706(2). The CASA court itself observed that “whether the Administrative Procedure Act
L1153@P45: authorizes federal courts to vacate federal agency action” is a “distinct question” from the limits
L1154@P45: of equitable relief under the Judiciary Act of 1789. CASA, 606 U.S. at 847 n.10 (citing 5 U.S.C.
L1155@P45-46: Case 1:26-cv-13799-FDS Document 50 Filed 09/14/26 Page 46 of 4847
L1156@P46: § 706(2)); see also id. at 873 (Kavanaugh, J., concurring) (“Going forward, . . . different district
L1157@P46: courts may . . . grant or deny the functional equivalent of a universal injunction . . . by
L1158@P46: preliminarily setting aside or declining to set aside an agency rule under the APA.”).
L1159@P46: The First Circuit has affirmed that view. In Woonasquatucket River Watershed Council
L1160@P46: v. U.S. Dep’t of Agric., the court rejected a categorical limitation on § 705 as a “mistaken
L1161@P46: understanding” of the statute’s postponement authority: the ability to provide relief beyond the
L1162@P46: named parties. 2026 WL 2279789, at *21-23 (1st Cir. Aug. 7, 2026) (rejecting arguments that
L1163@P46: § 705 was coextensive with traditional equitable authority). And other courts have concluded
L1164@P46: that § 705 authorizes relief beyond the named parties. See, e.g., Venezuelan Ass’n of
L1165@P46: Massachusetts v. United States Citizenship & Immigr. Servs., 2026 WL 2255272, at *5 (D. Mass.
L1166@P46: Aug. 5, 2026) (“[T]he Supreme Court decision in CASA does not limit the scope of relief under
L1167@P46: the APA.”); Career Colls. & Schs. of Tex. v. U. S. Dep’t of Educ., 98 F.4th 220, 255 (5th Cir.
L1168@P46: 2024) (“[T]he scope of preliminary relief under Section 705 aligns with the scope of ultimate
L1169@P46: relief under Section 706, which is not party-restricted.”). This Court therefore has the statutory
L1170@P46: authority to stay the Final Rule in its entirety.
L1171@P46: Of course, simply because this Court has the broad authority to exercise relief does not
L1172@P46: mean it is necessary or appropriate to exercise it. See United States v. Texas, 599 U.S. 670, 702
L1173@P46: (2023) (Gorsuch, J., concurring in the judgment) (“[A] district court should ‘think twice—and
L1174@P46: perhaps twice again—before granting’ such sweeping relief”” because of concerns such as
L1175@P46: judicial overreach, forum-shopping, and separation of powers). The question is whether
L1176@P46: considerations of administrability, efficiency, and uniformity are sufficient to outweigh factors
L1177@P46: counseling judicial restraint.
L1178@P46-47: Case 1:26-cv-13799-FDS Document 50 Filed 09/14/26 Page 47 of 4848
L1179@P47: Such is the case here. Plaintiffs represent almost 600 public and private institutions. But
L1180@P47: there are more than 5,000 higher-education institutions in the United States. Limiting relief to
L1181@P47: the parties represented would require maintaining parallel regulatory regimes and making
L1182@P47: repeated and potentially inconsistent determinations of whether a particular student or institution
L1183@P47: falls within the scope of the order. Such a regulatory regime would be further complicated by
L1184@P47: the fact that students regularly transfer between institutions or pursue joint degrees. In this case,
L1185@P47: nationwide relief—which, again, is permitted by § 705—prevents chaos and confusion that a
L1186@P47: party-specific order would inevitably generate. The Court will therefore grant the motion for a
L1187@P47: preliminary injunction to the extent it seeks to postpone the effective date of the Final Rule.
L1188@P47: IV. Conclusion
L1189@P47: For the foregoing reasons, plaintiffs’ motion for APA § 705 relief, a preliminary
L1190@P47: injunction, or, in the alternative, summary judgment, is GRANTED to the extent that it seeks to
L1191@P47: postpone the effective date of the Final Rule pursuant to the Administrative Procedure Act, 5
L1192@P47: U.S.C. § 705. To the extent that plaintiffs seek vacatur of the Final Rule, summary judgment, or
L1193@P47: other relief, the motion is DENIED without prejudice to its renewal.
L1194@P47: So Ordered.
